CC1.1: Management establishes expectations for ethical behavior and follows through when conduct falls short.
Code of conduct, communications, acknowledgements and appropriate follow-up records.
CC1.2: Oversight provides an appropriate independent perspective on the design and operation of internal control.
Oversight responsibilities, meeting records, challenge and follow-up decisions.
CC1.3: The organization defines responsibilities and reporting lines that support its control objectives.
Organization chart, delegated authority and role descriptions.
CC1.4: People performing control responsibilities have the competence and support needed for their roles.
Role requirements, training/experience records and competence evaluations.
CC1.5: People are held accountable for carrying out their assigned control responsibilities.
Assigned control owners, performance expectations and follow-up records.
CC2.1: The organization uses relevant, reliable information to support the way controls are designed and operated.
Control information sources, quality checks and management reporting.
CC2.2: People inside the organization receive the information they need to perform their control responsibilities.
Internal policies, control communications and escalation paths.
CC2.3: Relevant external parties receive or provide information needed to support internal control.
Customer/supplier communications, reporting channels and relevant agreements.
CC3.1: Objectives are clear enough to identify and assess the risks that could prevent their achievement.
Service commitments, system requirements and documented objectives.
CC3.2: Identify and assess risks to the organization's objectives and determine how they should be managed.
Risk methodology, scoped assessments and response decisions.
CC3.3: Consider how fraud could affect the achievement of objectives when evaluating risk.
Fraud-risk considerations, scenarios and related control decisions.
CC3.4: Assess changes that could materially affect the control environment or system commitments.
Change-impact assessments, new-service reviews and risk reassessments.
CC4.1: Evaluate whether controls are present and functioning, using ongoing or separate evaluations appropriate to the organization.
Monitoring reviews, control evaluations and documented conclusions.
CC4.2: Communicate control deficiencies to responsible people and track timely corrective follow-up.
Finding records, remediation Actions, escalation and validation decisions.
CC5.1: Select control activities that respond to the risks affecting objectives.
Risk-to-control decisions, control descriptions and owner approvals.
CC5.2: Establish technology-related control activities that support the achievement of objectives.
Technology control descriptions, configurations and operation records.
CC5.3: Put control activities into practice through policies and procedures that explain expectations and execution.
Approved procedures, assigned responsibilities and dated execution records.
CC6.1: Protect logical access to the system and information against unauthorized use.
Access-control design, enforcement configurations and coverage reviews.
CC6.2: Establish and authorize identities before granting the relevant system access.
Identity registration, approval and provisioning records.
CC6.3: Change or remove access as responsibilities and authorization change.
Access reviews, role-change approvals and deprovisioning records.
CC6.4: Restrict physical access to the facilities and assets relevant to system protection.
Physical access rules, access lists, visitor records and reviews.
CC6.5: Protect information when assets are retired, transferred or otherwise removed from service.
Retirement procedures, sanitization records and disposal verification.
CC6.6: Protect the system's external boundaries against inappropriate access and activity.
Boundary architecture, firewall/access configurations and exception records.
CC6.7: Protect information as it moves between systems, locations and external parties.
Transfer procedures, encryption/channel settings and handling records.
CC6.8: Prevent or detect unauthorized or malicious software that could affect system objectives.
Software protections, deployment coverage and detection follow-up.
CC7.1: Identify configuration weaknesses and vulnerabilities that could undermine the system.
Configuration reviews, vulnerability results and investigation records.
CC7.2: Monitor the system for anomalies that could indicate a threat to its objectives.
Monitoring coverage, alert rules and dated triage records.
CC7.3: Evaluate security events and decide whether they require incident response or other corrective action.
Event analysis, incident criteria and escalation decisions.
CC7.4: Respond to identified security incidents through the organization's established process.
Incident procedures, timelines, response actions and communications.
CC7.5: Recover from incidents and restore operation in a controlled way.
Recovery plans, restoration records, validation and lessons learned.
CC8.1: Authorize, assess, test and implement system changes in line with the organization's control design.
Change requests, approvals, testing and deployment records.
CC9.1: Manage the risks of business disruption that could affect system commitments and requirements.
Disruption risk analysis, continuity arrangements and exercise results.
CC9.2: Manage risks introduced by vendors and business partners that support the system.
Supplier assessments, agreements, assurance reviews and follow-up.
A1.1: Understand and manage capacity so the system can meet its availability commitments.
Capacity monitoring, forecasts, thresholds and resulting decisions.
A1.2: Provide operating safeguards that support the availability of the infrastructure and services in scope.
Environmental protections, backup arrangements, maintenance and resilience records.
A1.3: Test recovery arrangements to understand whether they support availability needs.
Recovery test scope, results, identified gaps and follow-up validation.
C1.1: Identify and protect confidential information throughout the parts of its lifecycle covered by the system commitments.
Confidentiality classifications, handling controls and lifecycle records.
C1.2: Dispose of confidential information according to the organization's commitments and requirements.
Retention/disposal rules, execution records and verification.
PI1.1: Define the information and processing specifications needed for the system to produce its intended results.
Processing specifications, data definitions and agreed requirements.
PI1.2: Accept inputs that meet the system's quality and authorization needs.
Input validation rules, authorization records and rejected-input handling.
PI1.3: Carry out processing as intended and identify or resolve processing errors.
Processing controls, reconciliation records and exception resolution.
PI1.4: Produce and deliver outputs that meet the system's processing requirements.
Output checks, delivery records and exception follow-up.
PI1.5: Protect stored inputs, processing data and outputs so processing integrity can be maintained.
Storage controls, retention settings and integrity verification records.
P1.1: Communicate the organization's relevant personal-information practices and purposes to the affected people.
Privacy notices, publication/version records and applicable delivery evidence.
P2.1: Explain relevant choices and consent options for personal-information processing.
Choice/consent notices, interfaces and communication records.
P3.1: Collect personal information in line with the stated purposes and applicable commitments.
Collection forms, purpose/data maps and collection controls.
P3.2: Obtain and retain explicit consent where the organization's collection practices require it.
Consent mechanism, recorded decisions and withdrawal handling.
P4.1: Use personal information consistently with the purposes and commitments governing it.
Purpose-to-use mapping, access restrictions and use reviews.
P4.2: Retain personal information according to the purposes and commitments that justify keeping it.
Retention rules, assigned owners and retention execution records.
P4.3: Dispose of personal information through appropriate secure handling when retention ends.
Disposal procedures, execution records and verification.
P5.1: Provide appropriate access to personal information after verifying the requesting person's identity.
Subject-request procedure, identity checks and response records.
P5.2: Handle requests to correct or amend personal information through an established process.
Correction requests, decisions, changes and response records.
P6.1: Disclose personal information consistently with the relevant consent and stated purposes.
Disclosure rules, consent context and approved disclosure records.
P6.2: Retain records that explain authorized disclosures of personal information.
Disclosure logs, recipient information and authorization context.
P6.3: Record and address unauthorized disclosures rather than treating them as ordinary data sharing.
Disclosure incident records, investigation and corrective follow-up.
P6.4: Address privacy responsibilities when third parties receive personal information.
Third-party commitments, agreements and oversight records.
P6.5: Establish how third parties communicate relevant personal-information disclosure issues.
Contractual notification responsibilities and received notification records.
P6.6: Maintain a process for evaluating and carrying out applicable breach notifications.
Breach assessment, notification decisions and communication records.
P6.7: Support applicable disclosure-accounting requests with appropriate records and responses.
Request handling, disclosure accounting and response records.
P7.1: Maintain personal information with the quality needed for its intended purposes.
Data quality checks, correction records and ownership decisions.
P8.1: Handle privacy complaints and monitor whether privacy practices follow the organization's commitments.
Complaint records, privacy reviews and corrective follow-up.

groups.CC1: Typical management controls assign governance responsibilities and demonstrate how expectations are communicated, applied and followed up. Distinguish the control's design from evidence that people actually performed it.
groups.CC2: Typical management controls identify who needs information, its source and the communication channel. Retain evidence that useful information reached the intended audience.
groups.CC3: Typical management controls define risk-assessment responsibilities and triggers, record decisions and connect identified risks to responses.
groups.CC4: Typical management controls evaluate operation, identify deficiencies and track corrective decisions through validation.
groups.CC5: Typical management controls explain who performs the activity, its scope, trigger or frequency and how exceptions are handled. A policy alone does not demonstrate operation.
groups.CC6: Typical management controls cover the relevant access paths and information lifecycle. Check enforcement, authorization records and exceptions in the actual system boundary.
groups.CC7: Typical management controls connect detection to evaluation, response and recovery. Retain dated records showing actions and decisions during the observation period.
groups.CC8: Typical management controls establish change responsibility, review, testing and release handling. Check ordinary and emergency paths and any exceptions.
groups.CC9: Typical management controls connect disruption or third-party risks to resilience decisions, agreements and ongoing follow-up.
groups.A1: Typical management controls connect availability commitments to capacity, resilience and recovery arrangements and retain operating and test results.
groups.C1: Typical management controls identify confidential information, its handling rules and lifecycle responsibilities, including disposal.
groups.PI1: Typical management controls define expected processing, validate inputs and outputs and track exceptions to resolution within the system boundary.
groups.privacy: Typical management controls connect the stated privacy practice to accountable owners, request or event handling and appropriately protected records. Use minimized examples rather than unnecessary personal information.
